derived_from: originally docpluck normalize.py steps A3a + A3 (docpluck v2.4.126). Those steps were DELETED in docpluck v2.4.129-v2.4.130; effectcheck is now the only implementation. See SPEC.md 'Status change, 2026-08-21'.
description: Language-neutral conformance corpus for numeric separator normalization. Both the Python (docpluck) and R (effectcheck) implementations must produce `expected` for every `input`. See SPEC.md.

Clinical-trial arm counts are written events/total with a slash, so '/' must be in T1's trailing boundary set. Without it the first count kept its comma, the arm regex's \d+ stopped at the comma, and arm1_events came back 234 instead of 1234 -- a silently wrong event count feeding the risk-ratio recomputation.

cases.input: The mean was M = 12,34 and the statistic t = 1234,56.
cases.expected: The mean was M = 12.34 and the statistic t = 1234.56.
cases.note: European decimals with TWO OR MORE integer digits. The discriminator is the digit count AFTER the comma (1-2 = decimal, exactly 3 = thousands), not before it. A draft of this port required exactly one digit before, copying docpluck A3, and silently stopped converting these -- a regression the previous implementation did not have.

cases.input: The test was reliable, t(1,197) = 2.31, p = .021.
cases.expected: The test was reliable, t(1197) = 2.31, p = .021.
cases.note: A t-test has exactly ONE df, so this is a thousands separator (df = 1197), not a df pair. Same shape as F(7,140) but the opposite answer -- the difference is test arity, which is statistics-aware and therefore effectcheck's layer, not the context-free spec's. MetaESCI E8 (2026-04-11): t(2,758) became t(2.758) and one article dropped 47 rows.
Kruskal-Wallis H also takes one df. Same reasoning as t.
F df pair. Must survive both rules intact.

cases.input: As shown by Smith, 1992, the effect replicates.
cases.expected: As shown by Smith, 1992, the effect replicates.
cases.note: No digit before the comma, so neither rule applies.
Leading zero means European decimal, not a thousands group -- T1 guard 1 rejects it, D1 converts it.

GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS: a mean of 1234, or a European 1.234? Resolved toward thousands, the right default for English APA output, but it is a default and not a proof. Changing this is a semantic decision requiring a spec version bump.

DIVERGENCE, found by effectcheck's suite and filed back to docpluck. A European decimal is routinely followed by the LIST comma. docpluck A3's lookahead omits ',', so it leaves '2,21' alone and a parser reads 2 -- a silent 10x error. effectcheck admits ',' in the lookahead; this is safe because the lookbehind already excludes a preceding digit (which is what blocks CI pairs) and T1 has already removed thousands groups. docpluck should adopt this.
Same divergence inside a CI. Both bounds are European decimals separated by a list comma.

cases.input: Across 1,182 participants the effect was d = 0,80.
cases.expected: Across 1,182 participants the effect was d = 0.80.
cases.note: Two conventions in ONE sentence, which is itself contradictory: 'd = 0,80' is a decisive EUROPEAN decimal marker, but '1,182' uses an ENGLISH thousands separator. Because the conventions are mutually exclusive, the decisive marker sets the document locale to European -- and under that locale '1,182' is exactly the shape structure cannot decide (1182 grouped, or 1.182 as a decimal). It is therefore PRESERVED verbatim and the row carries the ambiguity. An earlier expectation of '1182' predated locale inference and assumed shape-only resolution; silently picking either reading here would be a guess presented as a value.
A head noun (Experiment/Study/Table/Item/Condition...) followed by an integer list. The comma is a real comma. Both effectcheck and docpluck previously produced 'Experiments 1.2'.
Same class, different head noun.
Note 1,5 is exactly the shape of a European decimal -- only the head noun distinguishes it.
Longer list. Previously produced the INCONSISTENT 'anchors 1.2,3,4,5' -- only the first pair converted.
A coded variable, not a decimal. 'coded 0,1' would otherwise read as a decisive European marker and mis-set the whole document's locale.
Integer-only bracket pair is an index, not a CI. Distinguished from a CI by the absence of decimal points.
Same, parenthesised.
A DOI is an identifier. Previously corrupted to '.45.6'.
Period-thousands WITH comma-decimal. Self-identifying: no locale knowledge needed. Previously produced the unparseable '1.234.56'.
Space as the thousands separator.
Swiss apostrophe grouping.
Comma-thousands WITH period-decimal. Also self-identifying.

cases.expected: In 12.5% of cases the effect held.
cases.note: '%' was missing from the terminator whitelist, so this silently failed to convert. The fourth boundary character to bite us after '.', '/', '-'.
'-' was missing too, so only the SECOND number converted -- an inconsistent result within one range.

cases.input: Der Effekt war d = 0,80. Die Stichprobe war N = 1,234 Personen.
cases.expected: Der Effekt war d = 0.80. Die Stichprobe war N = 1,234 Personen.
cases.note: d = 0,80 is a DECISIVE European marker (operator-guarded leading zero). It establishes comma-as-decimal for the document, so N = 1,234 must NOT be read as 1234 thousands. Preserved and flagged rather than coerced.

cases.input: The effect was d = 0.80. The sample was N = 1,234 participants.
cases.expected: The effect was d = 0.80. The sample was N = 1234 participants.
cases.note: d = 0.80 is a DECISIVE US marker, establishing comma-as-thousands, so N = 1,234 resolves to 1234.
No decisive marker anywhere. Falls back to the documented default (thousands, correct for English-language APA output) but the row must carry an ambiguity flag rather than presenting as verified.

REAL corpus string. A reference-list volume and page range. Admitting a space after the comma in T1 fused these into '3424-453'. Corpus evidence: among 2,984 digit-comma-digit occurrences, the space-then-3-digits shape is overwhelmingly reference-list furniture, not a grouped number.
REAL corpus string, same class. Became '54437-449'.
REAL corpus string. An RGB triple, not a number. Became '120120120'.

REAL corpus string: three genuine table counts, space-separated, each internally comma-grouped. Must ALL strip. Two separate bugs hit this: the plain-space alternative in the European full-notation rule matched '669 107,081' across the gap and produced '403.669107.081', and the same plain space in the LOCALE DETECTOR classified this English table as European, gating the thousands rule off entirely.
REAL corpus string. Numbered-citation superscripts glued to a word. The letter in the lookbehind blocks it.
REAL corpus string. A bracketed citation run -- integers only, so the index/tuple protection covers it.
REAL corpus string. Superscript citations after a sentence-final period; the '.' exclusion in the lookbehind blocks it.

REAL failure mode. A space inside an explicitly labelled COUNT is extraction damage, not a separator, so the narrow N/nobs rule repairs it -- while the general rule leaves the same spacing alone in prose. Without this, .pat_doc_N's digit run stopped at the comma and the document N became 1, status OK, with no df-based guard on a z/U/W test.

cases.expected: Der Unterschied war signifikant, t(48) = 2.31, p = .025, d = 0.74.
cases.note: A continental paper omits the leading zero exactly as APA does. D1 requires a digit BEFORE the comma, so this p-value matched nothing and was SILENTLY DROPPED (p_reported = NA) while the same clause's t and d converted normally.

cases.input: The effect was reliable, d = 0.74, 95% CI [0.45, 0.89].
cases.expected: The effect was reliable, d = 0.74, 95% CI [0.45, 0.89].
cases.note: D1b is scoped to a VALUE POSITION -- a comma directly after = < or > with NO space. A list comma and a CI pair both carry a space, so neither can match. Admitting them would fuse real numbers.

cases.input: A register chi-square, chi2(1) = 8.42, nobs = 1, 234, 567, was significant, p = .004.
cases.expected: A register chi-square, chi2(1) = 8.42, nobs = 1234567, was significant, p = .004.
cases.note: The repair loop's anchor was \d{1,3}, so it could only ever run ONCE: after the first join the prefix is four digits and the pattern stopped matching. The row published N = 1234 -- a wrong sample size, not a missing one.

REAL corpus string, 11 occurrences in one paper. The full-notation rule matched '7.944,11' as European (period groups, comma decimates) and rebuilt it as '7944.11', so the text read '95%CI=[7944.11.984]' and the interval was DESTROYED -- ciL and ciU both NA, status still OK. In genuine full notation the part after the comma is a TERMINAL fraction and cannot be followed by another decimal point plus digits.
Same class, same paper.

REAL corpus string, same paper. The comma introduces the CI's confidence LEVEL, so '0.008,95' was read as full notation and rebuilt into '0008.95' -- fusing the reported coefficient with the interval's level and destroying the effect size. The `(?!\.\d)` guard cannot see this shape because what follows the fraction is '%'.
The guard must not disarm the rule: a sentence-final period after the fraction is not another decimal, so genuine full notation still converts.
Multi-group European full notation.

cases.input: In Study 1 the effect was reliable, t(58) = 2.41, p = .035, d = 0.80. In Study 2 Welch's correction gave t(2,758) = 3,21, d = 0,45.
cases.expected: In Study 1 the effect was reliable, t(58) = 2.41, p = .035, d = 0.80. In Study 2 Welch's correction gave t(2, 758) = 3.21, d = 0.45.
cases.note: BOTH conventions are attested and neither dominates, so inference returns confidence='conflict' with decimal_mark=NA. The ambiguous d,ddd token t(2,758) must be preserved -- NOT stripped to 2758. Reading conflict as US published df=2758, N=2760 and a computed d=0.122 against a reported 0.45: a false WARN carrying a fabricated effect size on a correctly reported result. Note the operator-guarded 3,21 and 0,45 DO convert -- they are decisive European markers in their own right, and only the d,ddd shape is undecidable.

cases.input: The sample was N = 1,234 participants and the effect was d = 0,80.
cases.expected: The sample was N = 1,234 participants and the effect was d = 0.80.
cases.note: The N = 1,234 token is AMBIGUOUS and stays so. Contrast case locale-no-evidence-preserves (rule L2), whose IDENTICAL token resolves to 1234: the only difference is that this document also carries a decisive European marker (d = 0,80), which makes it conflicted rather than evidence-free. Both states set decimal_mark = NA, so an implementation that tests only the decimal mark cannot tell them apart and will strip this comma -- resolving an ambiguity it has no evidence to resolve.

cases.input: The rate was ~25%6,28 in that sample.
cases.expected: The rate was ~25%6,28 in that sample.
cases.note: Spec 1.5.0. A percentage followed by CITATION SUPERSCRIPTS. Reported by docpluck 2026-08-13 and reproduced at effectcheck HEAD, where it became '%6.28'. `%` is now in D1's lookbehind exclusions: a European decimal is never written immediately after a percent sign, so the exclusion costs no coverage.

cases.input: The value was 9999999,1 in that condition.
cases.expected: The value was 9999999,1 in that condition.
cases.note: Spec 1.5.0. Reported by docpluck 2026-08-13 as a SPEC-vs-CODE contradiction and reproduced: the SPEC said one digit before the comma, the code allowed (\d+), and this became 9999999.1. Resolved at four digits -- see SPEC.md rule D1.

Spec 1.5.0. The counterweight to the case above, and the reason the SPEC's original one-digit rule was NOT adopted: a continental paper really does write this, and a one-digit port silently stopped converting it.

cases.input: Erik. T. Frank 1,2 , Lucie Kesner 3 and others.
cases.expected: Erik. T. Frank 1,2 , Lucie Kesner 3 and others.
cases.note: Spec 1.5.0. Reported by docpluck 2026-08-13 and reproduced ('Frank 1.2'). The glued form is blocked by the letter lookbehind and a 3+ run by the width test; a two-element run separated by a SPACE fell through both. Keyed on the author-list punctuation that follows (' ,'), not on the name.

Spec 1.5.0. The control for the case above, and it caught a real defect in the first draft of that guard: with `\s*,` instead of a literal ' ,' this input was protected and a genuine European decimal stopped converting.

Spec 1.5.0. Reported by docpluck 2026-08-13 and reproduced ('v2.1451.52.'). A dotted version is shaped exactly like European full notation, so a trailing citation run fused with it. Versions are identifiers and are now lifted out alongside DOIs.

Spec 1.5.0. docpluck reported this as a false negative in the coded|dummy|scored vocabulary and was about to adopt that vocabulary because of it. The vocabulary was never the cause: each element of the protected run is a single \d, so the pattern matched the PREFIX '0,8'. A trailing (?!\d) fixes it.
